query: What two problems does the Multi-Level Feedback Queue scheduler try to solve?
expected_answer: MLFQ tries to optimize turnaround time (which normally requires running short jobs first, something the OS can't do without knowing job lengths in advance) while also minimizing response time for interactive users, since algorithms like Round Robin achieve good response time but poor turnaround time.
expected_facts: goal: optimize turnaround time
OS doesn't know job length in advance, unlike SJF/STCF
goal: minimize response time for interactive users
Round Robin reduces response time but is terrible for turnaround time

relevant_passages.quote: The fundamental problem MLFQ tries to address is two-fold. Firs t, it would like to optimize turnaround time, which, as we saw in the previous note, is done by running shorter jobs ﬁrst; unfortunately , the OS d oesn’t generally know how long a job will run for, exactly the knowledge tha t algorithms like SJF (or STCF) require. Second, MLFQ would like to mak e a system feel responsive to interactive users (i.e., users si tting and staring at the screen, waiting for a process to ﬁnish), and thus minimiz e response time; unfortunately , algorithms like Round Robin reduce response tim e but are terrible for turnaround time.

query: Why does MLFQ start every newly arrived job off at the highest priority level?
expected_answer: MLFQ doesn't know in advance whether a job will be short or long-running, so it first assumes the job might be short and gives it high priority; a genuinely short job then finishes quickly, while a long job gradually falls down the queues and reveals itself as batch-like.
expected_facts: scheduler doesn't know if a job is short or long-running ahead of time
new jobs are first assumed to be short and get high priority
a truly short job runs quickly and completes at high priority
a long job slowly moves down the queues over time

relevant_passages.quote: From this example, you can hopefully understand one of the major goals of the algorithm: because it doesn’t know whether a job will be a short job or a long-running job, it ﬁrst assumes it might be a short job, thus giving the job high priority . If it actually is a short job, it will run quickly and complete; if it is not a short job, it will slowly move down the queu es, and thus soon prove itself to be a long-running more batch-like proc ess.
relevant_passages.section: Example 2: Along Came A Short Job

query: What problem does periodically boosting all jobs back to the top queue solve, and how often does Solaris perform this boost by default?
expected_answer: Periodically boosting all jobs to the topmost queue is meant to prevent starvation, since without it too many interactive jobs could combine to consume all CPU time and leave long-running jobs starved; Solaris's default MLFQ table boosts priorities roughly every 1 second.
expected_facts: problem being solved is starvation of long-running jobs
too many interactive jobs can otherwise consume all CPU time
Solaris default configuration boosts priority around every 1 second
Solaris default uses 60 queues

relevant_passages.quote: First, there is the problem of starvation: if there are “too many” in-teractive jobs in the system, they will combine to consume all CPU time, and thus long-running jobs will never receive any CPU time (they starve).

Default v alues for the table are 60 queues, with slowly increasing time-slice le ngths from 20 milliseconds (highest priority) to a few hundred millisecon ds (lowest), and priorities boosted around every 1 second or so.

query: How could a process game the original MLFQ priority rules to grab an unfair share of the CPU, and what rule change fixed it?
expected_answer: A process could issue an I/O operation just before its allotment ran out (e.g., using about 99% of the allotment before yielding) to stay at the same priority level and nearly monopolize the CPU; this was fixed by rewriting the demotion rule so a job is moved down a queue once it uses up its allotment at that level, regardless of how many times it gave up the CPU.
expected_facts: attack: issue I/O just before allotment expires to stay at same priority level
running about 99% of the allotment before relinquishing lets a job nearly monopolize the CPU
new Rule 4 demotes a job once its time allotment is used up regardless of how many times it gave up the CPU

relevant_passages.quote: the following attack: before the allotment is used, issue an I/O op eration (e.g., to a ﬁle) and thus relinquish the CPU; doing so allows you t o remain in the same queue, and thus gain a higher percentage of CPU time . When done right (e.g., by running for 99% of the allotment before relinq uishing the CPU), a job could nearly monopolize the CPU.
Rule 4: Once a job uses up its time allotment at a given level (re-gardless of how many times it has given up the CPU), its priority i s reduced (i.e., it moves down one queue).

query: Why is the pattern of a wait followed immediately by a signal called a turnstile?
expected_answer: It's called a turnstile because it allows one thread to pass at a time, and it can be locked to bar all threads; when locked (its initial state) it blocks everyone, and once unlocked all n threads pass through it one at a time.
expected_facts: pattern is a wait and signal in rapid succession
named turnstile because it allows one thread to pass at a time
it can be locked to bar all threads
initial state is locked (zero)

relevant_passages.quote: This pattern, a wait and a signal in rapid succession, occurs often enough that it has a name; it’s called a turnstile, because it allows one thread to pass at a time, and it can be locked to bar all threads.

query: Why does moving the turnstile inside the mutex lock cause a deadlock in the bad barrier solution?
expected_answer: If the first thread enters the mutex and then blocks at the turnstile, the mutex stays locked so no other threads can enter, meaning count can never reach n and the turnstile will never be unlocked, which is a case of blocking on a semaphore while holding a mutex.
expected_facts: first thread can enter mutex and block at turnstile
mutex stays locked so no other threads can enter
count==n condition can never become true
turnstile never gets unlocked
general lesson: blocking on a semaphore while holding a mutex causes deadlock

relevant_passages.quote: Imagine that the ﬁrst thread enters the mutex and then blocks when it reaches the turnstile. Since the mutex is locked, no other th reads can enter, so the condition, count==n, will never be true and no one will ever unlock the turnstile.
In this case the deadlock is fairly obvious, but it demonstra tes a common source of deadlocks: blocking on a semaphore while holding a mutex.

query: With 5 threads at the barrier, what happens to the semaphore's value as threads wait and then one is released?
expected_answer: With n = 5 and 4 threads waiting, the semaphore value is -4 (the negated count of queued threads); when the 5th thread signals the barrier, one waiting thread is released and the semaphore increments to -3, but then no one signals it again so the remaining threads stay blocked, causing a deadlock.
expected_facts: n = 5, 4 threads waiting gives semaphore value -4
semaphore value equals negated number of threads in queue
5th thread signaling releases one waiting thread and increments semaphore to -3
no further signals occur, so remaining threads can never pass

relevant_passages.quote: An an example, imagine that n = 5 and that 4 threads are waiting at the barrier. The value of the semaphore is the number of threads i n queue, negated, which is -4. When the 5th thread signals the barrier, one of the waiting th reads is allowed to proceed, and the semaphore is incremented to -3.
But then no one signals the semaphore again and none of the oth er threads can pass the barrier. This is a second example of a deadlock.

query: What single change turns the flawed barrier code into a correctly working barrier?
expected_answer: The non-solution has each thread wait at the barrier without ever signaling it again, so only the nth thread's initial signal is available; the fix adds another signal right after the barrier wait, so as each thread passes it signals the semaphore to let the next thread through.
expected_facts: non-solution: nth thread arriving unlocks the barrier by signaling it
non-solution has threads only wait on the barrier, no further signal
fix adds another signal after waiting at the barrier
each passing thread signals so the next thread can pass

relevant_passages.quote: The ﬁrst n − 1 threads wait when they get to the barrier, which is initiall y locked. When the nth thread arrives, it unlocks the barrier.
The only change is another signal after waiting at the barrier. Now as each thread passes, it signals the semaphore so that the next thre ad can pass.
